headline: The U.S. Army has launched a competition to develop a new long-range missile, the Affordable High Speed Strike (AHSS), which could eventually be compatible with HIMARS launchers. A key requirement is a range of more than 1,000 kilometers, exceeding the expected range of the latest Precision Strike Missile (PrSM) variant, which is already entering mass production. The Army has not yet specified a particular missile design. Potential concepts include a conventional solid-fuel ballistic missile and a weapon using an air-breathing propulsion system. Technologies developed under the Hypersonic Attack Cruise Missile (HACM) program have also previously been discussed in connection with AHSS, although the program does not require the use of the HACM design. The goal is to develop a relatively inexpensive, high-speed weapon capable of striking high-value targets deep inside enemy territory. The requirements specifically call for the ability to attack hardened aviation infrastructure and other facilities supporting enemy air operations.

headline: The extended deployment of USS Abraham Lincoln (CVN-72) and reported supply problems appear to be tied in part to the loss of the Navy’s logistics hub in Bahrain early in the Iran war according to a report from the New York Times. Iranian missile and drone strikes heavily damaged the Naval Support Activity Bahrain, home of the U.S. Navy's 5th Fleet, forcing the Navy to shift much of its regional logistics support to Naval Support Facility Diego Garcia, roughly 2,200 miles from the carrier forces operating in the Gulf of Oman. The island subsequently became an Iranian target, with two ballistic missiles launched toward Diego Garcia on March 20; one fell short and a Navy ship intercepted the other. That logistical disruption has coincided with an unusually demanding deployment for Lincoln. The carrier has been at sea for nearly nine months without a liberty call, while supporting combat operations and the blockade of Iranian ports. Lawmakers have raised concerns about reported shortages of basic supplies and deteriorating crew morale. The Navy is now replacing Lincoln with the forward deployed USS George Washington (CVN-73), which is already transiting toward the Middle East. Another carrier, George H.W. Bush, has also been operating in the region for months.

headline: The U.S. Army has temporarily grounded Apache helicopter training flights following the deaths of two soldiers in an AH-64E crash near Fort Hood, Texas, on Wednesday. Chief Warrant Officer 2 Deontre T. Huey, 34, and Warrant Officer Seth L. Olmsted, 25, were killed when their Apache crashed in a rural field near Salado. The crash sparked a wildfire, but no buildings were struck. The Army has not identified a cause and says the stand-down will remain in place until investigators have a better understanding of the accident. The temporary grounding affects training flights, not necessarily the entire Apache fleet. The AH-64 remains heavily used by Army and National Guard units and has also seen combat during the Iran war, including an Apache reportedly shot down by an Iranian drone over the Strait of Hormuz in June.

headline: RT by @sentdefender: An Italian Eurofighter assigned to NATO’s Baltic Air Policing mission shot down a drone of unconfirmed, but likely Russian origin after it entered Latvian airspace Friday, according to NATO and Latvian authorities. Two Italian Eurofighters scrambled from Lithuania along with two Turkish F-16s from Estonia. One of the Italian jets identified and engaged the drone. Latvian forces are now searching for the wreckage near Rugāji, about 35 km from the Russian border, so the drone’s origin has not yet been established. The incident comes amid a growing number of drone incursions into Baltic airspace. Latvia says Ukrainian drones have entered the region several times this year, while officials also point to Russian electronic warfare as a possible factor causing Ukrainian systems to stray across borders. Before Friday's incident, Ukrainian forces had launched attacks against Russian ports near St. Petersburg. Russian authorities claimed to have intercepted 15 Ukrainian drones during those attacks. This is the third reported NATO interception of a drone in the Baltics in recent months, following a Romanian F-16 shootdown in Estonia in May and a French Rafale shootdown in Latvia in June.

headline: The Trump administration has asked the Supreme Court to allow construction of the White House’s $400 million ballroom to continue while it appeals a lower court ruling that halted the project, according to the Associated Press. The D.C. Circuit ruled 2-1 that Trump cannot proceed without congressional approval, finding that the president lacks unilateral authority to build the 90,000 square foot structure where the East Wing once stood. The administration argues the project is necessary for White House security, calling the injunction unlawful and warning that stopping construction would leave an active construction site that is harder to secure. The appeals court had exempted work necessary for White House safety. The Supreme Court is being asked to act before the lower court's ruling takes effect on Aug. 21. The administration says the project is already about 65% complete after 10 months of construction.

headline: The U.S. is reportedly asking NATO allies to document not just their defense spending, but their political alignment with the Trump administration as part of its review of the U.S. military presence in Europe, according to reporting from Bloomberg. A questionnaire sent to NATO members asks whether governments have been publicly supportive of U.S. foreign policy, restricted U.S. military access to their bases, purchased from U.S. defense contractors, or opposed Euro-preference procurement rules. It specifically references restrictions imposed by allies on U.S. operations in the Middle East and asks whether those restrictions could be reduced or eliminated. The questionnaire comes as Washington considers major reductions to U.S. forces and wartime capabilities in Europe, with the review expected to conclude by December. Allies reportedly view the questions as an attempt to link U.S. security guarantees to political loyalty, potentially marking a significant shift from the traditional NATO model, where collective defense has been maintained despite political disagreements among members.
